doc.title: Terri Lyne Carrington interviewed by Monk Rowe, Toronto, Canada, January 9, 2003

title: Born into a musical Boston family
summary: Carrington says she never saw another path; her grandfather and father played drums and saxophone, her father nurtured her timekeeping, and she grew up on blues-based jazz.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: You know the material I’ve read about you seems like your career path was decided fairly early in life? Is that true?

Well this may have something to do with it, as far as decided early, we have a lot to do in the way of fate but we can I think help direct it but there is also sometimes some universal power that directs it for you. So for me I never really saw anything else for me to do with my life other than play music and play drums because I started so young.
What was it in your household that helped direct you down that path?

Well my grandfather played the drums but he passed away shortly before I was born. And my father plays saxophone and drums a bit as well so he would set up his father’s drums every now and then and I would just start playing sometimes. And I think the first time I © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -2-
was able to keep time immediately and he said well let me help nurture and develop this because it seems like she may have some talent.
Did he play recordings for you?

Oh all the time. I mean I grew up listening to jazz. My father was a very well versed musician in the jazz community in the Boston area. He was the president of the Boston Jazz Society. His father was a great drummer in the Boston area as well. He would play with different musicians when they came through town. Like if Duke Ellington came through maybe in the forties and didn’t have a drummer for some reason he would call him. Or Fats Waller same thing. And Chu Berry. So then my father went to college and started playing with the rhythm & blues bands at that time in horn sections, with Ruth Brown and a little bit with James Brown and different people. So music was really in my household. And I’d listened to jazz since I can remember.
And was it mostly swing-based jazz that you were hearing?
I think a lot of times it was blues based jazz, like organ trios, Gene Ammons, Cannonball, that kind of stuff. My father really, his style of playing is Gene Ammons is a big influence on him.
So a lot of that style.
